name: Gorum
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Anderson, Gregory D. S. & Felix Rau. 2008. Gorum. In Gregory D. S. Anderson (ed.), The Munda Languages, 381-433. London/New York: Routledge. The stress statement is reported from Aze, F. Richard. 1971. Parengi (Gorum) phonemic summary. Poona: Deccan College & Summer Institute of Linguistics (mimeo), p. 35.
catalog_locator: p. 386 (Google Books volume 6GzxBwAAQBAJ; every saved feed hit for the passage carries the preview link pg=PA386), stress subsection of section 2 Phonology, immediately preceding '2.6 Morphophonology'; passage assembled from five overlapping Google Books
catalog_quote: According to Aze (1971: 35), in Gorum isolated words, that is, those produced in isolation or not embedded within a larger prosodic structure, stress is generally found in word-final position, if the final syllable is closed; otherwise, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable in Gorum nominal forms. Gorum verb forms exhibit a range of morpholexical complications that deviate from this idealized system.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation-form (isolated) words, stress falls on the final syllable when that syllable is closed (CVC); when the final syllable is open, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable — stated for nominal forms. Verb forms do not follow this cleanly because of morphological complexity. The reported pattern is thus a final-syllable-weight rule (heavy final attracts stress, otherwise penult), not a fixed position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; a search-within-volume query for "secondary stress" co-occurring with Gorum returns 0 hits in The Munda Languages.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Gorum verb forms exhibit a range of morpholexical complications that deviate from this idealized system.' The rule is hedged ('generally'). Hock & Bashir 2016 (snippet) add the second-hand caution that such Munda judgments (citing Aze 1971: 35 for Gorum) may rest on two- or three-syllable words only.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly restricted to 'isolated words, that is, those produced in isolation or not embedded within a larger prosodic structure' (citation forms), and the penult default is stated for nominal forms; verb forms are said to deviate. Nothing said about phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Gorum = Parengi = Parenga (Glottolog pare1266, ISO pcj); Anderson & Rau 2008 describe 'Gorum' and Aze's 1969-72 data come from Bhejaguda village, Koraput District, Odisha (Aze 1973: 235). No dialect split is at issue. Not to be confused with the Dravidian 'Parji'/'Parenga Parja' or with Gadaba (Gutob), both listed among the alternate names.

sources.note: Citation-in-another-work: per Anderson & Rau 2008: 383 and Rau 2011: 175, Zide (1963, 1982) distinguishes three glottal phenomena in Gorum (glottal stop, creaky voice written /H/, glottalized syllable-final obstruents) and treats glottal stop and creaky voice as segments, the obstruent glottalization as non-phonemic, 'Thus Zide does not assume any register in Gorum'; Rau 2011: 174 adds that per Zide 1982 Juray also has creaky phonation as a variant of the glottal stop. Likely the fullest treatment of Gorum phonation/suprasegmentals before Rau; whether it comments on pitch or stress is unknown.
